title: 22. Interview: Disaster Recovery
summary: Interview Q&A for Disaster Recovery — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Disaster Recovery interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Define RTO and RPO, and explain why they drive every DR architectural decision.
**Answer:** RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable elapsed time between a failure and full service restoration — "we must be back online in 4 hours." RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time — "we can lose the last 15 minutes of writes, but no more." These two numbers drive architecture because each DR strategy offers a specific (RTO, RPO) pair at a specific cost. Backup-and-restore gives (24h, 24h) at ~1× cost; pilot light gives (4h, seconds) at ~1.3× cost; warm standby gives (1h, seconds) at ~1.7× cost; active-active gives (minutes, seconds) at ~2× cost. The business commits to RTO/RPO targets per service tier based on the cost of downtime and the cost of data loss, then the architecture must meet those targets. A tier-1 revenue service with an RTO of 1 hour cannot use backup-and-restore (RTO 24h violates the target); an internal reporting tool with an RTO of 24 hours does not need active-active (waste of money). RTO and RPO are not technical choices — they are business commitments that the technical architecture must serve.

**Visual:**
```
   failure
     |
     +---> [detection + decision + execution + validation] = RTO
     |                                      total time to restore service
     |
     +---> [data lost since last good backup/replica] = RPO
                                            amount of data lost

   strategy matrix:
   backup-restore  RTO 12-24h  RPO 24h    1.0x cost
   pilot-light     RTO 1-4h    RPO sec    1.3x cost
   warm-standby    RTO 10-60m  RPO sec    1.7x cost
   active-active   RTO min     RPO sec    2.0x cost
```

### Q2. Compare backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, and active-active. When would you choose each?
**Answer:** Backup-and-restore takes nightly snapshots to durable storage (S3) and on disaster provisions a new environment and restores the backup. It is the cheapest (~1× cost beyond backup storage), with RTO of 12–24 hours and RPO up to 24 hours. Choose it for systems where downtime is tolerable: internal reporting tools, batch jobs, dev environments. Pilot light keeps a minimal version running in a second region — typically just the database, continuously replicated — with the app tier scaled to zero. On disaster, scale up the app tier and cut over. RTO is 1–4 hours, RPO is seconds to minutes, cost is ~1.3×. Choose it for tier-2 services that need faster recovery than backups but cannot justify full redundancy. Warm standby is a full but undersized replica running continuously and replicating, not serving traffic. On disaster, scale up and shift DNS. RTO 10–60 minutes, RPO seconds, cost ~1.7×. Choose it for tier-1 services with strict RTO. Active-active runs both regions live, and on disaster the surviving region absorbs the load. RTO minutes, RPO seconds, cost 2×. Choose it for global services with latency and sovereignty requirements in addition to DR.

**Visual:**
```
   backup-restore:    [primary] --nightly backup--> [S3]
                      disaster: provision new env, restore (24h)

   pilot-light:       [primary full] --repl--> [standby DB only, app=0]
                      disaster: scale app 0->100, promote DB (1-4h)

   warm-standby:      [primary 100%] --repl--> [standby 25%, running]
                      disaster: scale 25->100, DNS shift (10-60min)

   active-active:     [region A 100%] <--repl--> [region B 100%]
                      disaster: DNS shifts to B (minutes)
```

### Q3. Why must backups be geographically separated and immutable, and what real incidents prove this?
**Answer:** Backups stored in the same site as production are destroyed alongside production when the site fails — a fire, flood, or power event takes both. The 2021 OVHcloud Strasbourg fire destroyed one datacenter and damaged another; customers whose backups were only on the destroyed site lost everything, while customers with off-site backups recovered. Immutability (WORM — write once, read many) protects against ransomware that encrypts production and then reaches for backups to encrypt them too. The 2017 Maersk NotPetya attack encrypted 49,000 endpoints and nearly all production data; the company was saved by a single off-site backup of one domain controller that was in a different country and not reachable by the attacker. AWS S3 offers Object Lock for WORM semantics; Glacier Deep Archive provides cheap long-term immutable storage. The pattern is: nightly logical backups to an S3 bucket with Object Lock in a different region than production, with a retention policy of 30 days daily plus 12 monthly snapshots for long-term recovery. The cost is trivial (cents per GB-month for S3, fractions of a cent for Glacier); the protection is existential. Without geographic separation and immutability, backups are theatrical — they look like DR but cannot survive the disasters that actually destroy data.

**Visual:**
```
   BAD (single-site):
   datacenter fire destroys:
     - primary DB
     - local backups (in same site)
   => total data loss

   GOOD (off-site + immutable):
   primary DB (us-east-1)
       |
       +-- nightly backup --> S3 + Object Lock (us-west-2, different region)
       |                       immutable: ransomware cannot encrypt
       +-- monthly snapshot --> Glacier Deep Archive (eu-west-1)
                               retained 12 months, geo-separated

   Maersk 2017: 1 off-site DC backup saved the company
   OVH 2021:    on-site-only backups were destroyed
```

### Q4. What is a DR drill, and why are drills more important than the runbook itself?
**Answer:** A DR drill is a scheduled exercise that deliberately simulates a disaster — killing instances, severing networks, failing a region — and observes whether the system actually recovers within the targeted RTO and RPO. Drills are more important than the runbook because DR systems decay silently: a standby database that has not been promoted in 6 months may have hidden replication lag, a DNS TTL may have been raised accidentally, a deployment may have updated the primary but not the standby, an IAM role the failover depends on may have been deleted. The runbook says "step 3: promote the standby" but does not prove step 3 works. Netflix runs Simian Army chaos engineering in production continuously (random instance kills) and Chaos Kong quarterly (full region failover); Amazon GameLift runs weekly failover tests; Google's DiRT (Disaster Recovery Training) program simulates large-scale failures yearly. Drills also train the people — the on-call engineer who has run a drill recognizes the failure pattern and executes confidently, versus the engineer encountering it for the first time at 3 AM who improvises badly. The cost of drills is engineering time plus brief user impact if the drill goes wrong; the cost of not drilling is the false confidence that you can recover, revealed as false during a real disaster.

**Visual:**
```
   quarterly DR drill (Chaos Kong style):
   T=0     announce "drill: failing us-east-1 in 1 hour"
   T=1h    inject: stop all instances in us-east-1
   T=1h    observe: does DNS shift? does eu-west-1 absorb load?
   T=1h    measure: error rate, latency, actual RTO, actual RPO
   T=1h05  if green -> drill passes, restore us-east-1
   T=1h05  if red   -> rollback, file bugs, retry next month

   without drills:
   3 years pass with no regional failure
   on year 4, real failure: standby 6h behind, TTL 1h, deployment
     never reached eu-west-1 -> 4h outage, RPO blown
   "we had a runbook" was false confidence
```

### Q5. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication, and how does each affect RPO?
**Answer:** Synchronous replication commits a write to both the primary and the standby before acknowledging the write to the client. The standby is guaranteed to have every committed write, so on failover no data is lost — RPO is zero. The cost is latency: every write incurs the round-trip time between primary and standby, which for cross-region replication is 50–100 ms, devastating write throughput. Synchronous replication is used when consistency is non-negotiable: financial ledgers (Google Spanner's TrueTime, PostgreSQL synchronous_commit), distributed lock services, and any system where losing a write is worse than slow writes. Asynchronous replication acknowledges the write as soon as the primary commits, then ships the change to the standby in the background. Write throughput is unaffected, but there is a replication lag window (typically 1–5 seconds) during which the standby is behind. If the primary fails during this window, the unreplicated writes are lost — RPO equals the lag. Asynchronous is the default for most multi-region systems because the latency cost of synchronous is too high for interactive workloads. The choice is RPO=0 with slow writes (synchronous) versus RPO of seconds with fast writes (asynchronous).

**Visual:**
```
   SYNCHRONOUS (RPO=0, slow writes):
   client --write--> primary --replicate--> standby --ack--> primary --ack--> client
                                              ^-- must wait for this
   total write latency = local commit + round-trip to standby (50-100ms cross-region)

   ASYNCHRONOUS (RPO=lag, fast writes):
   client --write--> primary --ack--> client
                       |
                       +-- background: replicate to standby (1-5s lag)
   total write latency = local commit only (fast)
   failure window = lag (last 1-5s of writes may be lost)
```

### Q6. What should a DR runbook contain, and why must it be tested by someone other than its author?
**Answer:** A DR runbook is the document an on-call engineer follows during a disaster, and it must be specific enough that a stressed engineer at 3 AM can execute it without thinking. It should contain: detection criteria (what monitoring signals trigger DR — error rate > 5% for 5 minutes, primary unreachable for 2 minutes), decision authority (who can declare a disaster and authorize failover — typically a senior engineer or manager, because failover has business cost), step-by-step execution (exact commands with expected output and time estimates — "run `aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-id xxx`, expect 'promoting' response within 30 seconds"), validation (how to confirm health after failover — smoke test endpoints, error rate < 1% for 5 minutes), and rollback (how to undo if failover makes things worse). The runbook must be tested by someone other than its author because the author's implicit knowledge is not in the document — they know to "first check that the standby's parameter group matches the primary," but if that step is not written, the test engineer will discover it the hard way. The test produces corrections: missing steps, wrong commands, vague criteria. A runbook that has not been tested by a fresh engineer is a wish, not a procedure.

**Visual:**
```
   DR runbook structure:
   1. Detection:    alert X for N minutes -> trigger DR evaluation
   2. Authority:    IC (name + phone) approves failover
   3. Pre-checks:   standby lag < 10s?  DNS TTL < 60s?  standby healthy?
   4. Execution:    step-by-step commands with expected output + time
   5. Validation:   smoke test, ramp 5% -> 25% -> 100%, error rate < 1%
   6. Rollback:     if validation fails, undo steps in reverse

   why test by a non-author:
   author:        "step 3: promote the standby"  (knows to check param group)
   test engineer: "step 3 failed: param group mismatch"  -> adds step 2.5
   test engineer: "step 5: smoke test endpoint returns 404" -> fixes endpoint
   test engineer: "step 4 took 20 min not 2 min" -> updates time estimate
```

### Q7. What is the role of the incident commander, and how does organizational readiness affect RTO?
**Answer:** The incident commander (IC) is the single person who makes decisions during a disaster — declaring the incident, authorizing failover, coordinating the response — while others execute. Without an IC, the team debates in a Slack channel for 30 minutes while the system stays down; with an IC, the decision is made in 2 minutes and execution begins. The IC role is distinct from the engineer role: the IC does not type commands, they absorb information, make decisions, and communicate (internal Slack, external status page, customer notifications). The IC must have pre-delegated authority — a senior engineer or manager who can authorize a 30-minute maintenance window or a multi-thousand-dollar spend without further approval. Organizational readiness directly affects RTO because the human steps — detection (5–15 min), decision (10–30 min), validation (15–60 min) — often dominate the technical execution (5–60 min). A team with a trained IC, a rehearsed runbook, and a quarterly drill can execute the human steps in 15 minutes; a team improvising for the first time takes 2 hours. The 2021 Facebook outage was extended because engineers could not reach the routers (the BGP misconfiguration took down the internal tools used to fix it) — the human and tooling path was broken. RTO is a human and organizational metric, not just a technical one.

**Visual:**
```
   RTO breakdown (real-world):
   detection        5-15 min   (monitoring + acknowledge)
   decision         10-30 min  (IC declares, authorizes failover)
   execution        5-60 min   (runbook steps)
   validation       15-60 min  (smoke tests, traffic ramp)
   ----------------------------------------------
   total RTO        35 min - 2h45m   (humans dominate happy path)

   without IC:                      with IC + drill:
   debate in Slack  30 min          IC decides in 2 min
   "is it really down?" 15 min      drill proves pattern, IC trusts
   "who can authorize?"  20 min     pre-delegated authority
   total human time     65 min      total human time     10 min
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run a payments service on a single region with nightly backups. A regulator demands an RTO of 1 hour and RPO of 5 minutes. How do you close the gap?
**Answer:** The current architecture (single region, nightly backups) gives RTO of 12–24 hours and RPO of 24 hours — far short of the regulatory target. The gap is closed by moving to a warm-standby architecture in a second region. I would provision a second region (`us-west-2` if primary is `us-east-1`) with the full application stack deployed via the same Terraform modules, running at 25% capacity. The database would use Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables for asynchronous cross-region replication with sub-second lag, giving an RPO well under 5 minutes (typically 1–5 seconds). Route 53 would health-check the primary every 10 seconds with a 60-second TTL on the steering record; on failure detection, DNS shifts to the standby, the standby autoscales 25% to 100%, and the standby database is promoted — total RTO of about 5–15 minutes for users with fresh DNS, well within the 1-hour target. I would also retain nightly logical backups to an immutable S3 bucket in a third region for protection against logical corruption. The plan must include quarterly DR drills to prove the RTO and RPO are real, not theoretical. The cost is roughly 1.7× the current single-region spend, justified by the regulatory requirement.

**Visual:**
```
   CURRENT (fails regulator):
   single-region us-east-1 + nightly backup
   RTO 12-24h, RPO 24h  ->  does not meet RTO 1h / RPO 5min

   PROPOSED (warm-standby):
   us-east-1 (primary, 100%) --async repl (lag 1-5s)--> us-west-2 (standby, 25%)
   Route 53 health check 10s, TTL 60s
   on failure:
     detect 10-30s + decide 5min + execute 5min + validate 15min = 30min RTO
     RPO = lag = 1-5s  (well under 5min target)
   cost: 1.7x current, justified by regulatory requirement
   + immutable S3 backup in us-east-2 for corruption safety
   + quarterly drill to prove RTO/RPO real
```

### Q2. A junior engineer runs `UPDATE users SET role='user'` without a WHERE clause, and it propagates to all read replicas before anyone notices. How do you recover?
**Answer:** This is a logical corruption event, not an infrastructure failure, and replication has already propagated the bad UPDATE to all replicas — so failing over to a standby does not help. The recovery path is to restore from a recent backup and replay the legitimate writes since the backup. The steps: first, stop the bleeding (revoke the engineer's write access, freeze the application to stop new writes); second, identify the time of the bad UPDATE from database audit logs (say, T=14:32); third, restore the most recent nightly backup (from T=02:00) to a new database instance; fourth, replay the binlog or transaction log from T=02:00 to T=14:31 (stopping just before the bad UPDATE) — this recovers all legitimate writes between the backup and the corruption; fifth, cut over the application to the restored database; sixth, communicate to users (those who changed their role between T=02:00 and T=14:32 may see their change reverted, and a manual reconciliation may be needed). The RPO here is the time between the backup and the corruption (about 12 hours of legitimate writes), but the binlog replay recovers most of them. The deeper lesson is that logical corruption requires point-in-time recovery (PITR) from backups, which replication alone cannot provide — both mechanisms are needed in a complete DR posture.

**Visual:**
```
   T=02:00  nightly backup taken (good state)
   T=14:32  bad UPDATE: SET role='user' (no WHERE)
   T=14:32  propagates to all replicas (replication is fast)
   T=14:35  user reports "all admins are gone"
   T=14:36  freeze app, revoke engineer access
   T=14:40  restore backup T=02:00 to new DB instance
   T=15:30  replay binlog T=02:00 -> T=14:31 (stop before bad UPDATE)
   T=16:00  cut over app to restored DB
   T=16:30  communicate: ~30 users' role changes between 14:31-14:32 lost
            (manual reconciliation from audit log)

   lesson: replication cannot save you from logical corruption;
           you need point-in-time recovery (PITR) from backups.
```

### Q3. Your team has a DR runbook that has not been tested in 18 months. A regional outage hits. What goes wrong, and how do you fix it for next time?
**Answer:** What goes wrong is that the runbook describes a system that no longer matches reality. Over 18 months, the standby database was renamed, the IAM role the failover depends on was deleted during a cleanup, the DNS TTL was raised from 60 seconds to 1 hour during a "performance optimization," the application added a new external dependency (a third-party API key) that was never provisioned in the standby region, and the on-call engineer who wrote the runbook left the company 6 months ago. The team executes step 1 of the runbook and it fails (wrong database name); they improvise; step 4 fails (IAM role missing); they improvise; total recovery takes 6 hours instead of the planned 30 minutes, with several mistakes along the way. To fix it for next time, the team institutes quarterly DR drills: every quarter, in a maintenance window, they execute the runbook end-to-end against the standby and verify it works. Each drill produces corrections (updated database names, recreated IAM roles, fixed DNS TTLs, added missing dependencies). The drill is owned by a rotating engineer (not the original author) so the runbook is tested by someone without implicit knowledge. After a year of quarterly drills, the runbook reflects reality, the team has muscle memory, and the next real outage recovers in 30 minutes as planned. The cost is one weekend per quarter; the benefit is recovering from the next outage in 30 minutes instead of 6 hours.

**Visual:**
```
   18 months of drift (untested runbook):
   - standby DB renamed (runbook says old name)        -> step 1 fails
   - IAM role deleted in cleanup                       -> step 4 fails
   - DNS TTL raised 60s -> 1h                          -> failover 1h slow
   - new 3rd-party API key not in standby              -> app crashes
   - runbook author left company                       -> no implicit knowledge
   result: 6h outage instead of 30min

   fix: quarterly drill
   Q1 drill: catches all 4 issues above, runbook updated
   Q2 drill: catches 2 new issues (new service added), updated
   Q3 drill: passes cleanly, runbook matches reality
   Q4 drill: passes, team has muscle memory
   next real outage: 30min recovery as planned
```

### Q4. Your RPO target is 5 minutes, but monitoring shows replication lag spikes to 10 minutes during peak hours. What do you do?
**Answer:** An RPO breach during peak hours means the standby is not keeping up with the primary's write rate, and a failure during the spike would lose more data than the target allows. The diagnosis flows from "where is the queue forming?" I would check four layers. First, the primary's write rate during the spike — is it 10× normal? If so, the standby's apply rate is the bottleneck, and I would scale the standby's instance class to match the primary's. Second, the network throughput between regions — is the inter-region link saturated? CloudWatch or VPC Flow Logs shows this; if saturated, I would add AWS Direct Connect for dedicated capacity or compress the replication stream. Third, long-running transactions on the primary — a 5-minute transaction holds the replication position until it commits, blocking subsequent writes. I would identify and break up long transactions. Fourth, schema changes — a `CREATE INDEX` on a large table blocks replication. I would move schema changes to off-peak hours and use online schema change tools (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change). As an immediate mitigation while diagnosing, I would throttle the primary's write rate (rate-limit the application) to keep lag under 5 minutes, accepting brief user-facing latency. As a long-term fix, if peak write rates are predictable, I would pre-scale the standby before the peak (predictive scaling for replication capacity). The target is a hard contract; breaching it during peak is a DR incident, not a "wait and see."

**Visual:**
```
   replication lag spikes to 10min during peak (RPO target 5min)
        |
   diagnose:
   1. primary write rate?     -> 10x normal? scale standby instance class
   2. network throughput?     -> saturated? add Direct Connect / compress
   3. long transactions?      -> 5min txn blocks position -> break up
   4. schema changes?         -> CREATE INDEX blocking -> use gh-ost, off-peak
        |
   immediate mitigation:
   - throttle primary write rate to keep lag < 5min (accept user latency)
        |
   long-term fix:
   - predictive scaling: pre-scale standby before peak
   - target is a contract, not a "wait and see"
```

### Q5. Your company suffers a ransomware attack that encrypts production and reaches the on-site backup server. What does your recovery look like, and what was missing?
**Answer:** If the only backups were on the on-site server that the ransomware reached, the recovery is catastrophic — there is no clean backup to restore from, and the company must either pay the ransom (no guarantee of recovery) or rebuild from scratch (potentially fatal for the business). This is what happened to many Maersk-style victims before they had off-site immutable backups. If the company had off-site immutable backups (S3 with Object Lock in a different region, or Glacier Deep Archive), the recovery is: isolate the infected systems (disconnect from network, preserve forensics), provision a clean environment in a different region, restore the most recent clean backup (say, last night's), replay transaction logs if available, cut over the application, and verify the ransomware did not persist in the restored data (scan for backdoors, change all credentials). What was missing was immutability and geographic separation: backups that the ransomware could reach and encrypt are not backups, they are additional victims. The fix going forward is: all backups go to S3 with Object Lock (WORM — even root cannot delete during retention) in a region different from production; nightly logical backups plus continuous replication to a read-only standby; quarterly restore tests to verify the backups are usable; and an air-gapped copy (Glacier Deep Archive with no programmatic delete) for the worst case. The cost is trivial; the protection is existential.

**Visual:**
```
   BAD (what was missing):
   production (us-east-1) --backup--> on-site backup server (us-east-1)
   ransomware encrypts production, then reaches backup server, encrypts it
   => no clean backup, company faces ransom or rebuild

   GOOD (recovery path with immutable off-site):
   production (us-east-1)
       |
       +--nightly backup--> S3 + Object Lock (us-west-2, WORM)
       |                     ransomware cannot encrypt (immutable)
       +--monthly snapshot-> Glacier Deep Archive (eu-west-1, air-gapped)

   recovery:
   1. isolate infected systems (disconnect, preserve forensics)
   2. provision clean env in us-west-2
   3. restore last night's backup from immutable S3
   4. replay transaction logs if available
   5. scan restored data for backdoors, rotate all credentials
   6. cut over application, verify
   RTO ~12-24h, RPO ~24h (since last nightly backup)
```

### Q6. You are asked to design DR for a tier-3 internal BI tool. Leadership wants active-active. How do you respond?
**Answer:** I would push back by quantifying the mismatch between the service's value and the proposed DR investment. A tier-3 internal BI tool has a downtime cost of roughly "the analysts wait" — measured in inconvenience, not revenue. The appropriate RTO is 24 hours (analysts can wait until tomorrow) and RPO is 24 hours (the data is rebuilt from the source systems overnight). Backup-and-restore satisfies these targets at about 1× cost — nightly snapshot to S3, on disaster provision a new environment and restore. Active-active would deliver RTO of minutes and RPO of seconds at 2× cost — a 2× cost increase for a service where the business impact of an extra 23 hours of downtime is "the analysts wait a day." The math does not work. I would also point out that active-active brings operational complexity (conflict resolution, multi-region deployments, DR drills) that the team supporting a tier-3 tool is unlikely to have the bandwidth to maintain — the drills will be skipped, the runbook will drift, and the "active-active" posture will silently degrade into "two regions that both think they're primary." The right answer for tier-3 is backup-and-restore with tested restores (verify the backup is usable quarterly). I would propose reserving active-active for tier-1 revenue services where the business case justifies it. The CTO's instinct to "be resilient" is right; the application to a tier-3 tool is wrong.

**Visual:**
```
   tier-3 BI tool: downtime cost = "analysts wait"
   RTO target 24h, RPO target 24h
        |
   strategy matrix (filtered by tier-3 targets):
   backup-restore   RTO 24h  RPO 24h  1.0x  -> MEETS target, cheap
   pilot-light      RTO 4h   RPO sec   1.3x  -> exceeds, overspend
   warm-standby     RTO 1h   RPO sec   1.7x  -> exceeds, overspend
   active-active    RTO min  RPO sec   2.0x  -> exceeds, overspend + complex
        |
   recommendation: backup-restore + quarterly restore test
   cost: ~$0 beyond backup storage
   saves: 2x cloud bill + operational complexity the team cannot maintain

   tier-1 checkout-api: same analysis says active-active is justified
```

### Q7. During a DR drill, you discover that failover takes 45 minutes instead of the planned 5. The bottleneck is DNS — clients cache the old IP for 5 minutes even though TTL is 60 seconds. What is happening and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The issue is DNS resolver caching behavior that violates the TTL contract. Many ISP and corporate DNS resolvers ignore or cap TTLs — they cache records for 5, 10, or 30 minutes regardless of the published 60-second TTL, either for performance (fewer upstream queries) or misconfiguration. Some clients also cache DNS at the OS or browser level beyond the TTL (Chrome caches for 60 seconds minimum, some apps cache for the process lifetime). The result is that even with a 60-second TTL, a meaningful fraction of clients keep hitting the old (failed) region for 5–10 minutes after the failover, extending the effective RTO. The fixes are layered. First, lower the TTL further — 30 seconds or even 5 seconds on the steering record; some resolvers respect lower TTLs even if they cap higher ones. Second, use a low-TTL CNAME indirection: the apex record (long TTL) points to a CNAME (5-second TTL) that you can swap instantly; clients that re-query the CNAME get the new target quickly. Third, use a global anycast DNS provider (Cloudflare, Route 53, NS1) that has resolver-like presence close to users and respects short TTLs aggressively. Fourth, for clients that ignore TTL entirely, use application-level retry with a fresh DNS lookup — if the connection fails, the client re-resolves and may get the new region. Fifth, accept that some clients will be stuck for the cache duration and design the RTO target around the realistic worst case (10 minutes for TTL-ignoring resolvers) rather than the happy path (60 seconds). The lesson is that DNS TTL is a hint, not a guarantee; DR plans must account for resolver non-compliance.

**Visual:**
```
   planned: TTL 60s -> failover propagates in 60s -> RTO 5min
   reality: TTL-ignoring resolvers cache for 5-10min -> RTO 45min

   fixes (layered):
   1. lower TTL to 5-30s on steering record (some resolvers respect lower)
   2. CNAME indirection: apex (long TTL) -> CNAME (5s TTL, swappable)
   3. global anycast DNS (Cloudflare, Route 53) close to users
   4. application-level retry with re-resolve on connection failure
   5. plan RTO around realistic worst case (10min for ignoring resolvers)

   before:  happy path RTO 5min  vs  real RTO 45min  (9x miss)
   after:   realistic RTO target 10min, drill confirms 8min  (within target)
```

It is the cheapest (~1× cost beyond backup storage), with RTO of 12–24 hours and RPO up to 24 hours. Choose it for systems where downtime is tolerable: internal reporting tools, batch jobs, dev environments.

quiz.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication, and how does each affect RPO?

quiz.explanation: Synchronous replication commits a write to both the primary and the standby before acknowledging the write to the client. The standby is guaranteed to have every committed write, so on failover no data is lost — RPO is zero. The cost is latency: every write incurs the round-trip time between primary and standby, which for cross-region replication is 50–100 ms, devastating write throughput.
